catalog_quote: The "tone" system of Tahgish comprises two levels, a low and a high, but I have the impression that there are likewise atonal syllables. In fact I have the impression that each word has a given tone level, either high or low, which applies to anly [sic] the "full" syllables, all others being atonal. The atonal syllables seem to occur mostly before the tone, but once the tone level is set it continues through the rest of the word. Atonal syllables at the end of a word are always affixes. This situation is somewhat parallel to that of some interior Salish languages, e.g. Shuswap, in which there are syllables with one of three "full" vowels and syllables with a reduced vowel ... new_statements.rule_in_words: No source states where word stress falls. Tagish is described as a tone language: two tone levels (high vs. low) on 'full' syllables, with reduced/atonal syllables (mostly prefixes before the tone-bearing part, and final affixes); each word is said to carry one tone level that persists to the end of the word. The 1994 practical orthography marks low tone with a grave accent (Tagish Literacy Workshop 1994: 5), i.e. a low-marked system, while the YNLC alphabet chart as summarised on Wikipedia marks high tone; neither says anything about stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Marsh flags his own record as sketchy (one elderly rememberer, 3 weeks in 1953) and says the prosodic features 'need further investigation'; his phoneme sheet adds 'length possibly prosodic (suprasegmental) rather than phonemic'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('each word has a given tone level'), based on elicited citation forms and a comparative wordlist; no phrase-level statement.
new_statements.identity_note: Marsh 1959 data are from Patsy Henderson (Carcross, 1953), a rememberer who had not used the language for 40 years; Leer/Golla/McRoy/YNLC materials are from Angela Sidney and Lucy Wren (Carcross/Tagish). All are the same Tagish variety (tagi1240); Marsh's spelling 'Tahgish'. Tagish is sometimes treated as a dialect of a Tahltan-Kaska-Tagish complex (Tahltan tahl1239, Kaska kask1239).

The pp. 69-71 passage is also verbatim: p. 69 (scan p-03, right column bottom, my own 110 dpi render) '..in others the constricted/nonconstricted contrast develops into a…
new_statements.relation_note: Same type as the existing Marsh 1959 statement (tone language, two levels, no stress placement) and consistent with the YNLC low-tone marking; adds the diachronic detail that Tagish low tone reflects Proto-Athapaskan constricted vowels. Nothing on stress, so the catalog's empty rule stands. The listed archive.org open_url (handbookofnortha0006will) is a lending-only item (access-restricted, not reachable by automated download; alternate handbookofnortha0006unse also restricted), so the chapter was read from the ANLA open scan CA961KG1981 of the same printed pages, which is the same work.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No statement about word stress or accent for Tagish (or any Northern Athapaskan language; the chapter's only 'accent' is 'pitch accent phenomena' in Carrier/Babine, p. 83). Tagish is described as a tone language whose tone arose from Proto-Athapaskan vowel constriction: constricted vowels carry low tone in Tagish and Tahltan (high tone in Kaska).
new_statements.exceptions: none; the chapter notes only that the tonal reflex of constriction differs by dialect (low in Tahltan and Tagish, high in Kaska)
new_statements.identity_note: Krauss & Golla treat Tagish (Bennett and Tagish Lakes area, last speakers in the bilingual Tlingit-Athapaskan community at Tagish, Yukon) as one of three dialects of a single Tahltan-Kaska-Tagish language and state the Tagish-specific tone reflex separately from Tahltan and Kaska; their data sources are G. Marsh 1956 and Golla 1976 fieldwork. Marsh's 'Tahgish' (Carcross, Patsy Henderson, 1953) is the same variety.

sources.locator: ms. p. 6 = PDF p. 45 (scanned in, pg-45); see also the 'Tahgish Phonemes' sheet at PDF p. 32
sources.note: Ms. p. 6 (PDF p. 45): Tagish has a two-level tone system (low, high) plus 'atonal' syllables; each word carries one tone level that applies to its 'full' syllables and, once set, continues through the rest of the word; atonal syllables occur mostly before the tone and word-final atonal syllables are always affixes. Contrasts this with Shuswap, which 'has no tone but rather a weak stress'; no statement about a Tagish stress position. Data: 3 weeks in Aug. 1953 with one rememberer (Patsy Henderson, 75).
